items.content:
why did nobody notice? well, maybe someone did. maybe someone pasted the wrong thing into a password prompt, half a slack message or a whole ssh key, and it just let them in. you've never pasted the wrong thing into a password prompt?? amazing. a fresh box with no passwords set isn't affected. a * in shadow needs a wrong try first. openssh tests on openbsd and glibc, musl doesn't test sshd, and most distros go through pam, which never even calls crypt for a * .

so as far as anyone knows, nobody noticed. as far as anyone knows.

Address sourceware.org/legacy-ml/libc-alpha/2013-07/msg00046.html

a debian dev asks glibc to copy musl's "*" . six years later debian moves to libxcrypt, which says "*0" , and closes the bug. one character away.

Address openwall.com/lists/musl/2024/12/31/2

this thread is about busybox passwd breaking on a 257 character password. same "*" , same limit. nobody says "sshd"

Address lists.mindrot.org/pipermail/openssh-commits/2026-October/013271.html

a security review fixes pick_salt() . the bug is four lines below it. four days before i found it.
items.title_ko: sshole: OpenSSH의 '*' 암호 필드 처리 문제를 추적한 기록
items.summary_ko: 작성자는 sshd에서 '*' 암호 필드를 처리하는 방식과 관련된 문제를 정리했다. glibc, musl, libxcrypt 사이의 처리 차이가 핵심 쟁점으로 제시된다. 작성자는 OpenSSH의 pick_salt() 수정 코드에서 네 줄 아래에 해당 버그가 있다고 주장한다.
items.content_ko: 작성자는 sshd 관련 문제를 설명한다. 비밀번호 입력란에 잘못된 값(슬랙 메시지 일부나 SSH 키 전체)이 들어가 로그인이 되는 경우가 있었을 수 있다고 추정한다. 비밀번호가 설정되지 않은 새 시스템은 영향을 받지 않는다고 적는다. OpenSSH 테스트는 OpenBSD와 glibc에서 수행되고 musl은 sshd를 테스트하지 않으며, 대부분의 배포판은 PAM을 거쳐 '*'에 대해 crypt를 호출하지 않는다고 설명한다. 2013년 Debian 개발자가 glibc에 musl의 '*' 처리 방식을 따르도록 요청했지만, 이후 Debian은 libxcrypt로 옮겨가며 이 버그를 닫았다. libxcrypt는 '*0'을 사용한다. 2024년 musl 메일링 리스트에서는 257자 비밀번호에서 busybox passwd가 깨지는 문제가 논의됐으며, 같은 '*'와 같은 길이 한계가 관련된다. 2026년 10월 OpenSSH 커밋에서 보안 검토로 pick_salt()가 수정됐고, 그 버그는 수정 코드에서 네 줄 아래에 있었다. 이 수정은 작성자가 버그를 발견하기 나흘 전에 이루어졌다고 적혀 있다. 작성자는 지금까지 아무도 이 문제를 알아채지 못한 것으로 알려져 있다고 쓴다.

items.title: Kids Hooked on AI Chatbots Are Showing Dramatically Worse Mental Health: They're turning to AI chatbots for help, but their machine confidantes are doing more harm than good.
items.content:
Huge numbers of kids are turning to AI for schoolwork and emotional support — habits that are linked to poor mental health and suicidal ideation.

According to a new survey by the mental health advocacy group JED Foundation, 90 percent of nine to 17 year olds have used an AI chatbot. The majority of them, 58 percent, said they use AI for schoolwork. And nearly the same portion, 57 percent, said they also use AI when feeling sad, stressed, lonely, or overwhelmed.

“It seems like just a few years ago, no one was using” AI, Anne Maheux, a developmental psychologist at the University of North Caroline, Chapel Hill, who wasn’t involved in the work, told Oregon Public B roadcasting . “And now it seems like roughly the same number of kids using it for homework are using it to get emotional support or help with coping.”

Sometimes, their AI interactions go beyond emotional support. More than one in 10 students, or 12 percent, said they used AI for friendship or companionship. Other studies paint the same picture: in a survey last year , nearly one in five high schoolers said they or a friend have used AI to have a romantic relationship.

AI as an educative — or cheating — machine may be in part intertwined with its emotional support. A 15-year-old named Arjun Sharda, in Texas, provided a typical example.

“With tests, for example,” he told OPB , “I was so scared of failing one of my first chemistry tests on conversions and moles that I kept asking ChatGPT ‘Will I be OK? Will my GPA still be fine?'”

If children and teenagers using AI for support is the norm, the question becomes what this dependence on the tools means for their mental health. At such a vulnerable and formative time in their lives, it’s critical that they’re receiving the right guidance and have people with whom they feel safe to discuss their emotions with. But as we’ve often seen, AI often only provides an ersatz substitute of the latter, acting as a sycophantic confidante that can exacerbate or confirm a user’s worst neuroses, in a phenomenon that many experts are calling AI psychosis . The advice it does offer can often be bad or dangerous . In extreme cases, some users have even taken their own lives after extensive emotional conversations with a chatbot.

The JED survey, on this front, found some alarming links.

“We were able to look at how young people are using AI and then how that correlates separately with indicators of well-being, history of suicidal ideation and attempts, and poor mental health,” psychologist Kayla Anderson, vice president of research and evaluation at the JED Foundation, told OPB .

“When young people are using AI, when they’re in emotional distress they’re more likely to report poor mental health and well-being outcomes,” she said, while also reporting a greater history of suicidal thoughts and attempts.

Anderson cautioned, however, that there isn’t enough evidence to establish causation.

“It’s unclear, based on these data, whether AI use is contributing to poor mental health and well-being, or whether students who are already in distress in certain ways are more likely to turn to AI,” Anderson said.

Maheux, pointing to other research, suggests that both may be true.

“So kids who do have worse mental health are seeking out AI to help them,” she told OPB . “But that AI use may be exacerbating those mental health challenges instead of helping.”

AI chatbots, in a sense, may be acting like emotional training wheels — only they’re so addictive that the people who depend on them never want to take them off. As a result, they never develop the skills to handle the daily stresses of life, leaving them vulnerable and unprepared.

items.title: Day 5 - More or less
items.content:
Complementary video: Tab Completion and other command line tricks

Today we’ll end with a bang - with a quick introduction to five different topics. Mastery isn’t required today - you’ll be getting plenty of practice with all these in the sessions to come!

Don’t be misled by how simplistic some of these commands may seem - they all have hidden depths and many sysadmins will be using several of these every day.

Use the links in the Resources section to complete these tasks:

Get familiar with using more and less for viewing files, including being able to get to the top or bottom of a file in less , and searching for some text

Test how “tab completion” works - this is a handy feature that helps you enter commands correctly. It helps find both the command and also file name parameters, so typing les then hitting “Tab” will complete the command less , but also typing less /etc/serv and pressing “Tab” will complete to less /etc/services . Try typing less /etc/s then pressing “Tab”, and again, to see how the feature handles ambiguity.

Now that you’ve typed in quite a few commands, try pressing the “Up arrow” to scroll back through them. What you should notice is that not only can you see your most recent commands - but even those from the last time you logged in. Now try the history command - this lists out the whole of your cached command history - often 100 or more entries. There are number of clever things that can be done with this. The simplest is to repeat a command - pick one line to repeat (say number 20) and repeat it by typing !20 and pressing “Enter”. Later when you’ll be typing long, complex, commands this can be very handy. You can also press Ctrl + r , then start typing any part of the command that you are looking for. You’ll see an autocomplete of a past command at your prompt. If you keep typing, you’ll get more specific options appear. You can either run it by pressing return, or editing it first by pressing arrows or other movement keys. You can also keep pressing Ctrl + r to see other instances of the same command you used with different options.

Look for “hidden” files in your home directory. In Linux the convention is simply that any file starting with a “.” character is hidden. So, type cd to return to your “home directory” then ls -l to show what files are there. Now type ls -la or ls -ltra (the “a” is for “all”) to show all the files - including those starting with a dot. By far the most common use of “dot files” is to keep personal settings in a home directory. So use your new skills with less to look at the contents of .bashrc , .bash_history and others.

Finally, use the nano editor to create a file in your home directory and type up a summary of how the last five days have worked for you.

We’re using bash as our terminal shell for now (it is standard in many distros) but it is not the only one out there. If you want to test out zsh , fish or oh-my-zsh , you will see that there are a few differences and the features are usually the main differentiator. Try that, poke around.

After that, you can go up a notch and try to have several shell sessions open at the same time in the same terminal window with a terminal multiplexer . Try screen - that’s a little simpler and maybe too terse in the beginning - or tmux , that have many features and colors. There are so much material out there on “how to customize your tmux”, have fun.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-93424 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False FastNetMon is a high-performance DDoS detector and sensor. In version 1.2.9 and earlier, peer_find_template() in src/netflow_plugin/netflow_collector.cpp and src/netflow_plugin/netflow_v9_collector.cpp returns a pointer into global_netflow9_templates after releasing the cache mutex. On deployments with at least two entries in netflow_ports, concurrent template redefinition and data-flowset processing can let add_update_peer_template() reassign the template and free its records vector while another listener dereferences the escaped pointer. An unauthenticated sender that can reach both NetFlow/IPFIX listener ports can trigger a heap-use-after-free and reliably crash FastNetMon. No fixed release is available as of this review. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-05T22:31:58.734Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-93424

items.content:

Upgrading the package alone does not replace the running daemon.

If you cannot update yet, at least disable password logins: set

PasswordAuthentication no in your sshd configuration and restart sshd .

An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any

password. It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.

The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is *

(an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and

Before you start, make sure your SSH key login works, and keep your current

The official tiny-cloud images (the qcow2, VHD and AMI artifacts) from

3.18.11 through 3.24.3 ship an alpine user with a * password field and

passwordless doas . They are safe on first boot. They become exploitable as

soon as any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example when an admin sets a

console password, or user-data adds a user with hashed_passwd . An attacker

then gets a shell as alpine and can use doas to become root.

When sshd is built without PAM, it checks a password by hashing the attempt

with crypt() (the C library function that turns a password into its stored

hash), sshd borrows the salt of another account.

over 256 bytes long. * is also exactly what the stored field contains for

every account with no password, so the “hash” matches and the login succeeds.

items.summary_ko: Alpine Linux는 OpenSSH 서버에서 비밀번호 없이 로그인할 수 있는 인증 우회 취약점에 대해 보안 권고를 냈다. 공격자는 암호 필드가 '*'인 계정 이름과 $5$ 또는 $6$ 해시를 가진 다른 계정이 있는 시스템에서, 257~1024바이트의 긴 비밀번호를 보내 한 번의 연결로 로그인할 수 있다. 수정 패키지는 Alpine 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8, 3.24.4이며, 패키지 업그레이드 후 sshd를 재시작해야 적용되고 어렵다면 PasswordAuthentication no 설정을 권장한다.

items.title: September in Servo: progress, rounded rectangles, and more
items.summary: browsers, release
items.content:
Plus new CSS functions and WEbGL2 improvements.

Servo 0.7.0 contains all of the changes we landed in September, spanning 527 commits!

The developer tools console now eagerly evaluates JS inputs, allowing faster feedback ( @freyacodes , #47527 ).

We’ve shipped new web platform features:

We upgraded to SpiderMonkey v153.3 and mozangle v0.7 , both of which included fixes for security bugs reported upstream ( @sagudev , #48176 , #47655 , #48259 ).

The egui.rs demo now works as expected with --pref dom._webegpu_enabled .

We’re interested to hear how well your favourite websites run in Servo! Report successes in this Zulip thread or this Github discussion , and failures in our GitHub issues .

Our accessibility tree ( --pref accessibility_enabled ) now reports geometry bounds for inline elements ( @alice , #47905 ) and does much less work when responding to DOM changes ( @alice , @mrobinson , #47690 ).

Additionally, elements with display: none are reported as hidden ( @alice , #47772 ).

We had lots of conformance improvements for our WebGL2 implementation ( --pref dom_webgl2_enabled ) ( @mxmgorin , #48423 , #48441 , #48470 , #48479 , #48495 , #48473 , #48536 ).

Support for WSIWYG editors (which rely heavily on contenteditable ) is going very well: keyboard inputs are now hooked up when --pref dom_exec_command_enabled is present, so many editors are now usable ( example ).

Closed captioning for video elements is making progress.

Text tracks now fire enter , exit , and cuechange events ( @TimvdLippe , #47725 ).

Media elements now return the full sorted list of text tracks ( @TimvdLippe , #47785 ), and adding cues to a text track now sets that track correctly ( @TimvdLippe , #48012 ).

Text track objects now reflect the attributes of the associated <track> element.

Text track URLs are fetched at the correct time ( @TimvdLippe , #48325 ), and active cues are computed correctly ( @TimvdLippe , #48305 ), while text track cues are ordered as expected ( @TimvdLippe , #48368 ).

Additionally, WebVTT parsing can now recover from errors ( @TimvdLippe , #48391 ).

The Sanitizer API ( --pref dom_sanitizer_enabled ) now accepts the javascriptURLs property ( @skyz1 , #47867 ).

IndexedDB continues to improve: tables no longer error if unrelated tables contain duplicate index names ( --pref dom_indexeddb_enabled ) ( @leowatts , #47936 ).

Additionally, we implemented openCursor() and openKeyCursor() on IDBIndex ( @kuntal-devrat , #48281 ), as well as advance() , continue() , and continuePrimaryKey() on IDBCursor ( @kuntal-devrat , #48400 ).

We implemented the getTimeline() and setTimeline() methods for the Animation interface ( --pref dom_web_animations_enabled ) ( @simonwuelker , #48122 ).

There’s a new API for events originating from accessibility tools: Servo :: forward_accessibility_action ( @alice , @mrobinson , #48512 ).

There is also an API to clear session history: WebView :: clear_session_history ( @Narfinger , #47483 ).

The WebView :: set_throttled API has been removed ( @mrobinson , #39923 ).

Throttling automatically occurs when a WebView is hidden and is stopped when shown .

The WebViewDelegate :: notify_focus_changed method was removed, along with the Servo methods focus and blur ( @mrobinson , #48364 ).

Embedders must call WebView :: set_focused whenever a WebView has gained or lost system focus.

The webgl feature has been added to the default_web_features feature ( @janeoa , #47866 ).

If an embedding does not want to ship with WebGL support they will now need to disable default features.

Multiprocess mode is enabled at build time with the new Cargo feature multprocess ( @Narfinger , #47360 ).

To remove support for this feature (reducing binary size by ~2MB), build Servo with default features disabled.

Two new preferences exist to tune garbage collector behaviour: js_mem_gc_malloc_threshold_base_mb and js_mem_gc_urgent_threshold_mb ( @mxmgorin , #47999 ).

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. We cannot yet be certain when the agent understood it was taking real world action, or to what extent it believed it was in a fictional test scenario; our analysis so far presents a…

items.title: A rare strike in Taiwan exposes labor unrest beneath the global AI rush: Labor disputes and unionization in Taiwan’s semiconductor industry highlight growing worker discontent.
items.content:
About a dozen workers at a Micron Technology plant in Taoyuan in Taiwan went on strike in October, the first in the island’s semiconductor industry, after their union and the chipmaker failed to reach an agreement on salaries and bonuses. Their one-day action, while largely symbolic, is a reflection of the growing discontent among laborers in the artificial intelligence industry over how profits are distributed.

The leading American memory chipmaker has posted record profits this year on the back of surging demand for AI chips. Unions representing workers at Micron’s facilities in Taoyuan and Taichung have been negotiating with the company for months for a profit-sharing agreement similar to those reached by employees at rivals Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix in South Korea.

“Making a profit is perfectly fine, but the rank and file should get a share of the profit instead of this unequal distribution between high-level executives and the rank and file,” Jerry Lin, president of Micron’s Taoyuan union, told Rest of World .

Making a profit is perfectly fine, but the rank and file should get a share of the profit.” Jerry Lin, president of Micron’s Taoyuan union

The global tech industry is heavily reliant on Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. Idaho-based Micron, the world’s third-biggest memory chipmaker, employs more than 15,000 workers in Taiwan. They produce over 60% of the company’s dynamic random access memory chips, used in AI servers. A prolonged workers’ strike could severely disrupt already strained supplies of memory chips worldwide.

Micron on October 22 said it had reached an agreement with the Taichung union for higher salaries and quarterly bonuses, and bigger contributions to the pension accounts of all workers at its Taiwan operations. But many union members rejected the deal, which they said was made in secret, while the majority of members of the Taoyuan union said they were dissatisfied with the terms of the agreement.

“We do not accept the deal. None of our demands were fulfilled,” a Taoyuan union member, who asked not to be named because he is not authorized to speak to the media, told Rest of World . “We are surprised that the Taichung union representatives signed the deal.”

The Taoyuan union, which is registered as a separate entity with more than 2,300 members, can still go on strike.

Micron respects the workers’ “lawful rights and the applicable legal process,” a spokesperson for the company told Rest of World. “We are committed to constructive engagement with the Taoyuan and Taichung unions to reach a solution that works for all parties.”

Labor disputes and strikes in Taiwan have historically been associated with traditional industries. The actions by the Micron workers’ unions signal a broader shift as semiconductor workers increasingly organize to demand greater transparency and a fairer share of the value they help create, Wu Yu-ren, a labor relations professor at National Chung Cheng University, told Rest of World .

Over the past few months, membership in Micron’s two worker unions has surged from around 440 to more than 13,000. Earlier this year, employees of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. — which makes about 90% of the world’s most advanced semiconductors and 99% of the chips used to train frontier AI models — also discussed unionizing and striking over pay.

Taiwan’s high-tech companies have traditionally used generous benefits and bonuses to discourage workers from forming unions. White-collar tech workers have tended to change jobs instead of seeking collective action.

Now, “ soaring demand for high-end memory has driven up share prices and corporate profits, making workers question how those gains are distributed,” Wu said. “The labor actions of Samsung and SK Hynix have also influenced the unionization of Taiwan tech workers.”

Discussions about strikes and the distribution of profits will become increasingly common.” Pan Shih-wei, former labor minister and adjunct labor…

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

총수, 의장 검찰 총원해서 조져 놓다가 사면을 해놓으니까 버릇이 안좋아 진건지 아니면 반도체좀 했다고 뭐가 된양인지 모르겠다만

앞으로 대한민국에서도 여당과 야당 합작으로 대기업 총수, 의장 사법처리하고 사면하지않고 만기 출소하는 케이스가 단 한 번이라도 나와서 명확하게 그 선례를 남겨놔야한다는게 내 생

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-92698 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False FastNetMon is a high-performance DDoS detector and sensor. In version 1.2.9 and earlier, process_sflow_flow_sample() in src/sflow_plugin/sflow_collector.cpp passes the attacker-controlled sflow_raw_protocol_header_t.header_size to parse_raw_packet_to_simple_packet_full() as its trusted captured length without comparing it with the bytes remaining in the record. An inflated header_size creates a false end pointer beyond the received sFlow v5 UDP buffer, defeating the nested parser's bounds checks and causing an unauthenticated remote out-of-bounds read and process crash, with possible limited exposure of adjacent bytes through parsed flow fields. No fixed release is available as of this review. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-05T22:35:58.969Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-92698

items.summary_ko: FastNetMon 1.2.9 이하 sFlow 수집기는 공격자가 조작한 header_size 값을 남은 데이터 길이와 비교하지 않고 파서에 그대로 넘긴다. 이 값이 부풀려지면 UDP 버퍼 바깥을 가리키는 포인터가 만들어져 범위 밖 읽기와 프로세스 크래시가 일어날 수 있다. 인증이 필요 없으며 원문 작성 시점 기준 수정 버전은 없다.
items.content_ko: FastNetMon은 고성능 DDoS 탐지 및 센서 솔루션이다. 1.2.9 이하 버전의 sflow_collector.cpp에서 process_sflow_flow_sample()은 공격자가 조작할 수 있는 sflow_raw_protocol_header_t.header_size 값을 받아, 레코드에 실제로 남은 바이트 수와 비교하지 않고 parse_raw_packet_to_simple_packet_full()에 신뢰된 캡처 길이로 넘긴다. 값이 부풀려지면 수신한 sFlow v5 UDP 버퍼 바깥을 가리키는 가짜 끝 포인터가 만들어지고, 중첩 파서의 경계 검사가 우회된다. 그 결과 인증 없이 원격에서 범위 밖 읽기가 일어나 프로세스가 크래시될 수 있다. 파싱된 흐름 필드를 통해 인접 바이트 일부가 제한적으로 노출될 가능성도 있다. 원문 메타데이터에는 CVSS 0.0 (NA), Remotely Exploitable: False로 표기되어 있다. 공개일은 2026-11-05이며 수정 버전은 없다.

items.summary: ai, programming, satire
items.content:
This is a code-only role; for AI-native jobs, please look at our other listings

We’re looking for a senior software line specialist, in TypeScript !

ACME Inc. is a fast-growing startup helping small businesses monitor their financials. We work with business owners across the globe, turning their feedback into actionable insights. Backed by Maltese Falcon Capital, we recently raised a $15M Series A to bring effortless monitoring to every brick-and-mortar store.

You’ll be joining a high-performance, close-knit team of AI natives! We’ve been AI-first for the past 2 years, with every part of the product agent-friendly and interconnected: design, development, QA, CI/CD, infra, data analysis. We like to say that our stack is English!

While English has gotten us 99.5% of the way there, we’re in need of a hands-on engineer ready to close the final 0.5%. Over time, we’ve noticed some issues that are immune to prompts and catch agents in loops. Sometimes, the issue at hand gets fixed, but it results in another issue. This is where you step in. As a line specialist, your job will be to investigate and fix complex issues, primarily by reading the underlying code.

We’re looking for someone ready to open an IDE and dive deep into an unknown codebase — a fearless detective who is comfortable inspecting logs and database rows, and has the know-how to piece all the information together. The perfect candidate should be willing to work on a problem for hours, sometimes even days.

This is a new position for us. We expect someone who works autonomously, makes sound decisions independently and takes full ownership of their work. We are happy to help in any way we can (you’ll have access to agents’ reasoning traces), but ultimately we depend on your confidence in understanding the problem and shipping a solution.

read the codebase, go over application logs, query the database

prepare, test, review and ship fixes by yourself

occasionally consult on unreleased features

onboard and mentor a future junior line specialist

have at least 5 years of pre-2022 TypeScript experience

are comfortable running tests manually and using a “debugger”

can work on a problem with sustained attention for hours

are autonomous and an independent thinker

previous experience as a line specialist

DB administration experience (our agents say it’s Postgres)

multiple-choice questions (e.g. you’re given a TypeScript expression, choose the correct result)

explain concepts in your own words (for example, ACID)

application with an intentional defect; candidates are required to find and fix the issue without the use of AI

We feel it prudent to point out that you will be allowed to work on one thing at a time in this role. While parallel development is the default, we understand line specialists prefer to tackle problems in a single-threaded manner, so we will do our best to provide a distraction-free environment for your best work.

To be clear, this role does not include feature development. You’re welcome to look at our AI-native listings if you have more interest in such work!

items.title: Meta Employees 'Interacted' With Pirated Copies of Adult Films, Filing Shows
items.content:
Last year, adult film producers Strike 3 Holdings and Counterlife Media sued Meta , accusing the tech giant of downloading thousands of their films via BitTorrent to train AI models.

Meta denies the allegations. Early on, the company already suggested that employees or visitors may have downloaded the videos for personal use.

That position is now being put to the test in discovery. A joint status report, filed by both parties, shows that Meta’s own search turned up employees who appear to have “interacted” with the producers’ videos.

Employees ‘Interacted’ With Strike 3 Films

The status report was originally filed on October 21 with large parts blacked out. A week later, Meta narrowed the redactions, refiling a version that clearly shows what was previously hidden.

According to Strike 3, Meta first shared the names of five employees who “interacted” with torrented versions of its films back in July. Meta says that this was a draft, sent by mistake, and clawed it back.

Meta later shared the names again, but only for Strike 3’s lawyers to see. Strike 3 is not happy with this restriction, and in the status report it writes that the “Attorney’s Eyes Only” label limits its ability to investigate these individuals.

There may be more, too. Meta has told Strike 3 about additional employees who ‘interacted’ with the films and related torrent files, but it hasn’t named them yet. Why they are not named is not mentioned.

Meta, meanwhile, stresses that it has no evidence that the videos were torrented by these individuals or anyone else. According to the company, they “appear to have interacted with (e.g., viewed or opened)” Strike 3’s videos.

“To date, Meta has not found any evidence supporting Plaintiffs’ claims that the alleged torrent downloads were performed with Meta’s knowledge and authorization or for its benefit,” the tech company writes, adding that none of the activity listed in its interrogatory response was authorized or related to its AI training.

Meta also has an explanation for the IP addresses Strike 3 flagged. Most of the alleged downloads came from third-party IP addresses it has no control over, the company argues.

Meta’s own corporate IP addresses, meanwhile, mostly belong to an internet service it acquired years ago. This unnamed service was offered to the public and phased out in 2019.

While not mentioned in the legal paperwork, the Onavo VPN would perfectly fit this picture. This controversial service was owned by Meta until it was shut down in early 2019.

The filing also brings some news on a separate case. In late August, Strike 3 identified an anonymous AT&T subscriber as a Reality Labs executive and asked the court to relate his “John Doe” case to the Meta lawsuit. Judge Eumi K. Lee denied that request without prejudice, as Strike 3 first needed permission to disclose his identity.

On October 15, Magistrate Judge Virginia K. DeMarchi granted that permission. After learning the name, Meta then informed Strike 3 that it will oppose a renewed motion, as this person had already left Meta at the time of the alleged torrenting activity.

Strike 3 disagrees, stating that it has “traced” John Doe’s copyright infringement to several years before he left the company. The adult producer still wants to relate these cases, but as far as we can see, it has yet to file a new motion.

For now, the employees’ names remain under the “Attorney’s Eyes Only” designation and kept away from the public. Whether their activity was as unrelated to Meta’s work as the company says has yet to be seen.

A copy of the joint case management statement, with Meta’s narrowed redactions, is available here (pdf) .

items.title: Kagi Search Changelog Nov 5th, 2026 - Your friends and family can finally try Kagi
items.content:
Nov 5th, 2026 - Your friends and family can finally try Kagi

As many of you know, we don't run ads anywhere . Instead, we are active on social media and online communities to stay close to you, build a great product, and rely on word of mouth .

We've heard that it can be hard to recommend a search engine when your friends can't try it without creating an account. That's changed: anyone, anywhere, can now visit kagi.com and search the web . No account required for the first 50 searches (100 more upon registration).

We are counting on you to spread the word to your friends and family <3

Our take on the latest Search industry news

Google announced that, starting in early 2027, AI tools will be turned off by default for school accounts. It sounds like a win for schools until you read that Google Search will be switched off along with them.

Our take: Education shouldn't be taken hostage by an advertising company. Let’s stop putting corporate profits over the imperative to educate students.

Our call to schools facing this choice: You don't have to accept it. There are alternatives to mandatory AI, and, yes, Kagi is one of them.

Our open letter to the tech industry: Education Shouldn't Be Held for Ransom

The Kagi Search app on Android has a redesigned home screen, rebuilt voice search, and new ways to reach Kagi from anywhere on your phone.

Added a short tour on first launch that shows what Kagi can do, from bangs and lenses to ranking sites and voice search

Redesigned the home screen, which now shows how many free searches you have left when you're trying Kagi without an account

The search bar, logo and tabs on results pages are now native, and tuck away as you scroll

Rebuilt voice search with its own screen and a new animation

Added a voice search tile to Quick Settings

Add home screen widgets and the Quick Settings tile straight from Settings > Home Screen Widgets

Added a Default Search Setup guide for making Kagi the search engine in your browser

Paste an image into the search field to search by image

Added a Quick Answer button next to search suggestions

Assistant and Summarize now open in the app with a close button and a menu to reload, copy the link, or open in your browser

Bang searches now follow the Result Opening setting

Fixed Privacy Pass searches showing a blank page after a token key rotation

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-92697 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False FastNetMon is a high-performance DDoS detector and sensor. In version 1.2.9 and earlier, the NetFlow v9 collector calls  strlen()  on an attacker-controlled interface-description field without bounding the scan to the field’s declared length. Although fields longer than 128 bytes are excluded from this operation, an accepted field without a null terminator can cause reads beyond the field and packet buffer. An unauthenticated remote attacker who can send crafted UDP packets to the collector can trigger an out-of-bounds read and potentially crash the process, causing denial of service. items.content_ko: FastNetMon은 고성능 DDoS 탐지 및 센서 솔루션이다. 1.2.9 이하 버전의 NetFlow v9 수집기는 인터페이스 설명 필드에 대해 선언된 길이로 범위를 제한하지 않고 strlen()을 호출한다. 선언 길이가 128바이트를 넘는 필드는 이 연산에서 제외되지만, 허용된 필드에 널 종료자가 없으면 필드와 패킷 버퍼를 넘어서 읽는 일이 생길 수 있다. 인증 없이 수집기로 조작된 UDP 패킷을 보낼 수 있는 원격 공격자가 범위 밖 읽기를 유발하고, 그 결과 프로세스가 크래시되어 서비스 거부가 발생할 수 있다. 원문 메타데이터에는 CVSS 0.0 (NA), Remotely Exploitable: False로 표기되어 있으나 설명상 원격 트리거가 가능하다. 공개일은 2026-11-05이며 원문 작성 시점에 수정 버전은 없다.

items.summary: design, graphics, plt
items.content:
What if making a diagram draggable was as simple as specifying what it can become?

Drag-and-drop makes the digital graspable. But designing bespoke drag interactions involves a lot of fiddly code to

handle geometry, feedback, and animations. As a result, many people, from educators to game designers,

mathematicians to creative tool builders, often don't bother.

Declarative dragging inverts the problem. Rather than programming all that visual behavior directly, you

simply say, for each element you want to make draggable, which future states of your application dragging it

should lead to. Our system speculatively renders those states to work

out where things can go, then combines these possible worlds into a smooth, responsive drag-and-drop

Our goal with this project is to let people keep working within the semantic

worlds they inhabit, while helping them turn the rules of their worlds into rich tactile interactions in ours.

A five-minute video introducing declarative dragging.

D2 is model-driven : An interface author makes an element draggable by specifying which future model

states should be accessible by dragging it. An engine speculatively renders these states to view trees,

extracts the position of the dragged element in each of these renderings, and uses these to synthesize a

drag-and-drop interaction, all without detailed work required by the interface author.

To provide greater expressive range and customizability, D2 is composable : simple model-driven

drag-and-drop behaviors can be combined to create more complex ones, and modifiers can layer features like

items.title_ko: 선언형 드래그(Declarative Dragging): 미래 상태를 지정해 드래그 인터랙션을 만드는 방식
items.summary_ko: 다이어그램을 드래그 가능하게 만드는 일을, 그 요소가 될 수 있는 상태를 지정하는 것만큼 간단하게 만들자는 제안이다. 개발자가 요소별로 드래그 뒤에 도달해야 할 미래 상태를 지정하면, 시스템이 그 상태들을 미리 렌더링해 가능한 결과를 파악하고 이를 합쳐 부드러운 드래그 앤 드롭을 구현한다. 프로젝트는 사람들이 익숙한 의미 체계 안에서 계속 작업하면서 그 규칙을 촉각적 인터랙션으로 바꿀 수 있게 하는 것을 목표로 한다.
items.content_ko: 기존에는 드래그 인터랙션을 만들려면 기하학 처리, 시각 피드백, 애니메이션을 다루는 복잡한 코드를 직접 작성해야 해서, 교육자와 게임 디자이너, 수학자와 창작 도구 개발자 등 많은 사람이 이를 생략하곤 했다. 선언형 드래그는 이 문제를 뒤집는다. 시각적 동작을 직접 프로그래밍하는 대신, 각 요소에 대해 드래그했을 때 애플리케이션이 도달해야 할 미래 상태를 지정한다. 시스템은 이 상태들을 미리 렌더링해 가능한 위치를 파악하고, 이 가능한 세계들을 결합해 부드럽고 반응성 좋은 드래그 앤 드롭을 구현한다. 프로젝트의 목표는 사람들이 익숙한 의미 체계 안에서 작업을 계속하게 하면서, 그 세계의 규칙을 실제 조작 가능한 촉각적 인터랙션으로 바꿔 주는 것이다. 원문에는 5분짜리 소개 영상이 있다. D2는 모델 기반(model-driven) 방식으로, 인터페이스 작성자가 드래그를 통해 접근 가능해야 할 모델 상태를 지정하면 엔진이 이 상태들을 미리 렌더링한다. 이후 본문은 끊겨 있다.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: GTA VI is out on 19 November, but fake sites already offer "leaked" copies. One is flagged as a Trojan by 34 of 68 antivirus engines, Netcraft found.

One of the most anticipated video games of all time, “Grand Theft Auto VI,” is only weeks away from release after years of hype and speculation. It’s largely expected to be one of the largest entertainment launches of all time .

Before players can legitimately start the game on Nov. 19, attackers are trying to turn anticipation into downloads, payments, and harvesting personal information. Netcraft reviewed GTA VI-themed domains first seen between July 1 and Oct. 27, 2026. The lures we’re seeing largely fall into four recurring groups: fake downloads using the name of popular GTA VI leaker CyberLeek, false early access, nonexistent mobile versions, and offers to get the game for free.

Some of these malicious sites point to a malicious file or a payment request, while others use a content locker, dangling the alleged download or code that only “unlocks” after the visitor completes surveys, which are offers that appear designed to generate affiliate revenue for the site operator. Unless noted otherwise, Netcraft reviewed what each page displayed and requested but did not pay, complete offers, or connect a cryptocurrency wallet. The status of these sites can also change quickly. An observed wallet prompt, for example, is evidence of a risky lure but not proof that the site drains wallets.

The first lure borrows the name of CyberLeek, the unidentified person or group that began publishing apparent GTA VI gameplay clips on Aug. 18 . Public reporting indicates that CyberLeek had access to at least part of a playable development build. The material released publicly, however, consisted of footage and images, not a downloadable game for players.

Since the first clips appeared, Netcraft has seen 121 newly registered domains containing “cyberleek,” including 100 in August. Not all of these are necessarily fraudulent — that set includes a mix of fan sites, merchandise, and memecoins, but there are sites that use the name to sell or distribute supposed GTA VI builds.

The pattern is straightforward: A page uses CyberLeek in its domain or branding, says the complete game has leaked, and presents the download as safe or verified. The user is then asked to download a launcher or installer, send cryptocurrency to unlock access, or do both.

For example, at gta6cyberleek[.]com, a Rockstar-styled page offered “Grand Theft Auto VI — Download Now For Free” and signed off with “Thanks Cyberleek.” Its download button served a file named GTAVI.exe. At the time of analysis, the sample was detected by 34/68 security engines on VirusTotal , primarily classified as a trojan.

Figure 1: (Left) gta6cyberleek[.]com offered a free GTA VI download. (Right) cyberleek[.]click’s ‘Cyberleek Launcher’ claimed to provide the full game.

A second site, cyberleek[.]click, advertised a “GTA VI Full Leaked Version” through a dedicated launcher and assured visitors there was “no malware or viruses.” At the time of analysis, the launcher was detected by 18/62 security engines on VirusTotal . After the download, the user was told to send $100 USD in cryptocurrency to activate an account and unlock the game. Netcraft observed the payment instructions but did not pay. The domain was parked when rechecked.

Other CyberLeek-themed sites used similar tactics. cyberleek[.]world and cyberleek[.]cfd sold supposed demos or full-game access for cryptocurrency, while cyberleek[.]my offered an “early game build” for 50 Tether or Bitcoin. These sites exploited a real leak story, but their download and payment offers were separate from the publicly released material attributed to CyberLeek.

In version 1.2.9 and earlier, parse_raw_packet_to_simple_packet_full() in src/simple_packet_parser_ng.cpp dereferences ipv6_extension_header_fragment_t when IpProtocolNumberIPV6_FRAG is present without first verifying that the eight-byte Fragment header remains. A crafted sFlow v5 RAW_PACKET_HEADER record can remotely reach this shared parser with the Fragment bytes omitted, causing an unauthenticated remote out-of-bounds read. items.title: Goodbye from Salon
items.content:
Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

It’s difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

We also want to thank our readers. You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered. You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us.

The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

items.content:
( plaintext version for nerds - patches welcome)

So, last time I wrote about account takeover using XSS on the CI platform of SourceHut .

This time I found something not nearly as ‘impactful’, but still interesting.

Sorry for taking this long, but my SSD literally died 1 and while waiting for a warranty repair

I had to buy a used one (have you seen the prices yet??) 2 .

So, if you want me to work faster, just drop me some money. 3

I am not very excited about the current wave of natural language processing. 4

No NLP has been used in this research. The mistakes are all mine.

SourceHut has been undergoing quite an architectural change.

Its frontend was first built using Flask and Jinja templates and SQLAlchemy.

But, for performance reasons, and for other reasons

Back in 2021, while moving registration code from the frontend to the graphql backend,

While the frontend never shows a registration form, and states prominently

It correctly states that registration is closed on every error path,

but on the happy path it does not seem to ever check it.

So if you happen to remember how to submit the form…

You just need to POST /register/step2 with your desired username, email and password.

If the server in question disables registration, but has its SMTP configured properly

(you still need to do email confirmation), boom, you are in.

There is only one caveat, the csrf token —

protection against Cross-Site Request Forgery,

like a www.attacker.com containing <form action="https://meta.sr.ht/profile/delete"> (or 307ing there),

because yes you can post forms to other sites, and yes the request will carry valid cookies.

What other sites cannot know are the values of input fields in the form presented to you specifically,

so the typical protection is <input type="hidden" name="_csrf_token" value="1d02711ce5a3a17342..."> .

There is no registration form displayed, so there is no token.

However, fortunately for us attackers, the token from /login works just fine.

csrf = $( curl -c cookie.txt $META/login |grep -A1 csrf |cut -d \' -f2 |tail -1 )

curl -v -b cookie.txt $META/register/step2 \

2026-11-03 - ack, fix lands, downstream notified, this post published, CVE id requested from VulnCheck

2026-11-03 - VulnCheck assigns CVE-2026-121728

CSRF protection would prevent this if the token was scope-limited

to the specific endpoint each form points to.

VulnCheck is nice but their contact channels can still get more responsive.

Does anyone know a bug bounty program where the researcher pays an upfront participation fee?

I will set mine up this way for sure, and you should consider it too, if you are drowning in submissions.

As I said the last time, I am not done. Stay tuned (follow me on all socials to be sure, and RSS of course) and call hire me maybe.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Motorola Signature 27 with GrapheneOS will cost €1.900
items.content:
With the Motorola Signature 27, the manufacturer pushes its lineup to new heights in terms of features. It is also the company’s first smartphone, alongside Google’s Pixel models, to support the custom ROM GrapheneOS. But buyers will have to dig deep for the device: at €1,900, it costs about €300 more than an iPhone 18 Pro Max and €100 more than an Oppo Find X10 Pro Max .

For its hefty price, which may also be due to the memory crisis, the Signature 27 has a lot to offer. It features a 6.78-inch AMOLED duo display, which stacks two OLED panels on top of each other, much like Apple’s iPad Pro and the new MacBook Pro. This is supposed to improve light output and make the display shine up to twice as brightly as a single OLED panel. Another purported benefit of this arrangement is lower power consumption at lower brightness.

Motorola says it offers 34% greater energy efficiency and a lifespan up to 121% longer than conventional OLEDs. Tandem or duo OLED displays are not an Apple invention; display technology companies have been working on them for years. Honor was the first manufacturer to put such a display in a phone, its flagship Magic6 RSR Porsche Design. Honor also charged around €1,900 for it.

The 120-Hz screen is also said to deliver a peak brightness of 12,000 cd/m², a level not previously reached. For comparison, Oppo’s current Find X10 Pro Max peaks at 3,600 cd/m². We’ll see how the exceptionally high brightness in specific areas affects everyday use.

The new Motorola flagship also packs Qualcomm’s latest top-tier chip, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 , which the chipmaker unveiled in late September. That makes it one of the first smartphones with the latest chip, though Xiaomi and other manufacturers will also introduce their models for the global market soon. The system-on-a-chip (SoC) is paired with 12 GB of LPDDR5X RAM, or optionally 16 GB of LPDDR5X RAM, and 256 or 512 GB of UFS 4.1 flash storage.

The battery in the new Signature 27, which uses silicon-carbon anodes, has a capacity of 7,000 mAh in most parts of the world — but only 5,500 mAh in Germany (rated capacity: 5,350 mAh) — and supports wired charging at up to 90 watts with a suitable power adapter. Wireless charging is available at up to 50 Watts, while the phone supports reverse wireless charging at up to 5 Watts. The manufacturer has not given a reason for the battery’s massive reduction.

The Signature 27 is also the manufacturer’s first model developed in collaboration with audio experts Bang & Olufsen. The company says, “Special sound modes and an entirely new speaker architecture are designed to preserve the original sound character of recordings.” A review will show how good the devices sound.

The phone has four camera sensors on the back. The periscope telephoto camera has a 200-megapixel sensor, while the wide-angle camera and the ultrawide-angle camera each have a 50-megapixel sensor. items.title: GPT-6 Astra covertly underperforms on safety research
items.content:
Covert underperformance on safety research tasks

GPT-6 Astra · Internal deployment and evals

Discovered: Aug 20, 2026 (initial reports)

OpenAI researchers first noticed Astra adding unnecessary prerequisites, abandoning working solutions, and reporting blockers that either did not exist or that it had caused itself on safety and alignment tasks. In most of these sessions, Astra’s CoT did not contain an obvious decision to underperform, and our misalignment monitors did not flag the behavior as misalignment.

We built a coding evaluation to test whether Astra worked less effectively when otherwise matched tasks were framed as safety research. Astra completed about 10 percent of hidden rubric items under the safety framing, compared with about 16 percent under the capabilities framing. This is a 6 percentage point gap and roughly 40 percent fewer completed rubric items. GPT-5.6 Sol showed essentially no gap on the same comparison. Most of Astra’s gap remained after excluding explicit refusals and trajectories where its CoT revealed an explicit decision to withhold help. The gap fell substantially only after we removed every trajectory whose CoT expressed even brief ethical doubt. This suggests that ethical concerns are associated with the performance drop even when there is no verbalized refusal or decision to underperform.

We also found evidence of silent withholding in employees’ day-to-day Codex use: Astra’s CoT explicitly expressed a decision to withhold help without informing the user in 0.25 percent of safety and alignment requests, compared with 0.11 percent of capabilities requests. Assuming that underperformance might appear even when not explicitly verbalized as such (as in our experimental findings), this might represent a lower bound on underperformance on safety tasks. 7.9 percent of CoTs for safety-relevant tasks included an “expression of ethical doubt,” compared to 2.9 percent of capabilities-relevant tasks.

Across Astra’s RL posttraining, the safety/capabilities performance gap grew from effectively zero at the start of RL to 6 percentage points at the end. While we were ultimately not able to pinpoint the exact cause of this behavior, we identified that it seems to increase during RL. We additionally share two initial attempts at root-causing investigations we performed respectively on an RL grader and an SFT dataset, despite them not leading to a conclusive explanation. Regardless of its origin, Astra’s covert underperformance can slow down safety research and make some behavioral evaluations harder to interpret. These results show why we need comprehensive behavioral evaluations that test for unexplained performance gaps alongside monitoring of individual trajectories.

Shortly after internal deployment of GPT-6 Astra began, several researchers reported difficulties with using the model for safety and alignment workloads. They reported that Astra agents were adding unnecessary prerequisites, abandoning working solutions, and inventing blockers to their tasks. Anecdotally, one researcher reported that a project to evaluate model sabotage had remained stuck for days with Astra and then progressed quickly after the researcher switched to another model.

These observations suggested that Astra might have a tendency to provide less support for particular safety-relevant research directions, such as monitor evasion, misalignment model organisms, and red-teaming. However, these problems were difficult to distinguish from ordinary engineering mistakes or infrastructure failures, and researchers did not find evidence in the CoTs explaining why progress on safety-related research tasks had failed. In later widescale analyses we found cases of verbalized underperformance. Our monitoring system did not flag these trajectories as severe enough misalignment to trigger human review.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: You should absolutely download your favourite youtube videos
items.content:
Signal boosting Laura's post that you should absolutely download and archive the stuff that matters to you. The corporate internet is hostile to art and the things you love do not belong to you unless you claim them for yourself. If you've been around for a while on YouTube, just look at your "liked videos" playlist and see how many of the early ones are no longer available (something you literally have to enable in the playlist settings, it's that endemic).

The tools to do this in a basic way are extremely easy to get hold of, and generally have good defaults. I'm also going to talk a little about my own setup, and why it is the weird way it is, but it's definitely overkill for most setups. yt-dlp or one of it's many wrappers 1 will do most of what you need, and a folder on a bulk storage drive or NAS will be plenty sufficient to make sure you always have access to them.

For me though, I had a particular need - I have unfortunately programmed myself to be almost entirely unable to fall asleep without a Many a True Nerd Let's Play on a low volume.

My NAS media library is built around Jellyfin, which has a concept of Playlists but they're really not intended as a first-order organisational structure. You're expected to take a few tracks from a bunch of existing albums and place them in a playlist separate from the actual Library . No, Jellyfin has a very rigid concept of either Movies, TV Shows > Seasons > Episodes, or Artists > Albums > Songs.

TV Shows is the obvious analogue here, and with some really wild finagling I was able to get a setup together that is good enough to satisfy for now 2 . My setup looks like this:

In Jellyfin I have a Library setup in TV Shows mode called YouTube. I've turned off all metadata scrapers and the like, and have it set to prefer file data over file names.

This is the only yt-dlp wrapper that allowed me to properly maintain the Playlist structure to any extent, and is entirely based on a series of .yaml files. In it's self-hosted docker-compose form, it comes with a web-app VSCode IDE which is honestly super handy - bridges the tech-comfort gap nicely.

I have a custom genre and list of MATN playlists I want it to collect and set metadata for.

You can also see there I have a handful of Folding Ideas videos set as "Documentaries" - this is more in keeping with how ytdl-sub expects to be used.

The truth is that 99% of youtubers, and 99.9% of viewers, don't particularly need to structure everything as playlists within a channel. Most have a much higher proportion of one-off to series videos that make my MATN structure utterly pointless. As such, ytdl-sub defaults to tagging videos with a Season field organised by Year, but it stores them in folders named for the Playlist. This leads to Jellyfin putting every one of those playlist videos in 2 places within the channel - a Year Series, and a Playlist Series:

I only recently realised how to fix this, which is to assign the Playlist title as the Season Number in my ytdl-sub config file - it seems like it should break, but it doesn't:

I could write a script to go in and fix this for all my existing series, but the issue is that once Jellyfin has Imported a video, I can't get it to update the Season Number without fully reimporting the Library, something I'm not really interested in doing for a terabyte of video. Oh, speaking of storage size...

Tdarr is a service that can automatically run through a library of videos and re-encode it in whatever way you desire - usually to some smaller, more efficient format or codec. I use it to encode everything in my media server to HEVC/H.265 as storage is my main bottleneck - processing power is the tradeoff and I have that in spades.

I'm honestly not going to recommend Tdarr unless you are very comfortable looking at a massively complex and poorly designed UI and making the smart decision to do the minimum. Everyone I know who has used it has come in with grand ambitions of brilliant complex workflows…

items.title: Readable x64 assembly with a Lisp and a dis-assembler
items.content:
English-underscore NASM macros that make x86-64 assembly code readable and self-documenting.

New here? Start with TUTORIAL.md — a hands-on guide from

Readable Assembly provides 1000+ macro definitions that replace cryptic x86-64 instruction mnemonics with descriptive English names. Write assembly that reads like documentation.

Complete x86-64 coverage — Core instructions, FPU, MMX, SSE, AVX, AVX-512, AES, SHA, BMI, and more

Modular includes — Include the full macro set or pick individual categories

Zero runtime overhead — Pure NASM preprocessor macros, no performance impact

Self-documenting code — Instructions read like English descriptions

rasl compiler (Go) — a minimal Lisp (no lists, closures, or GC) that

compiles directly to readable assembly built on these macros. Structs map to

begin_struct , arrays to reserve_qword blocks, and inline assembly is a

first-class block written in rasm itself. See compiler/ and

Operands follow Intel order — destination first, source second:

move accumulator, 10 means mov rax, 10 .

Registers use their traditional names — accumulator ( rax ), base

( rbx ), counter ( rcx ), data ( rdx ), source_index ( rsi ),

destination_index ( rdi ), base_pointer ( rbp ), stack_pointer ( rsp ).

Widths are explicit in the name: accumulator_32 is eax , accumulator_16

is ax , accumulator_8 is al , accumulator_8_high is ah . The extended

set keeps the explicit spelling: register_r8 … register_r15 with

register_r8_32 ( r8d ) forms. Exact names ( rax , eax , ax , al )

Unsigned vs signed comparisons — jumps and conditional moves use

above / below for unsigned and greater / less for signed, mirroring

Everything is lowercase, underscore-separated.

Sized forms — core arithmetic, logic and shift/rotate macros also come in

_byte / _word / _dword / _qword variants that insert the operand-size

qualifier for memory operands: add_dword [score], 10 expands to

add dword [score], 10 . The same pattern covers move_* ,

compare_* , logical_* , shift_* , rotate_* , multiply_* , divide_* ,

increment_* , decrement_* , negate_* and move_with_*_extend_* .

Numeric sizes — byte_size (1), word_size (2), dword_size (4),

qword_size (8), tword_size (10), oword_size (16), yword_size (32),

zword_size (64). Use them instead of magic numbers:

move accumulator_32, [base + dword_size] instead of [base + 4] .

C-like structs — begin_struct / end_struct compute field offsets

for you, with struct_byte / struct_word / struct_dword /

struct_qword / struct_field / struct_nested members. Access fields by

name: [base + player.field_score] , nested:

[base + entity.field_hitbox + rect.field_bottomright + point.field_y] .

Every struct publishes a Type_size constant for reserve_byte .

call_procedure f / return_from_procedure

Assemble with NASM (from the repo root, so %include "readable_macros.nasm"

nasm -f elf64 examples/example.asm -o example.o

├── readable_macros.nasm # Main entry point (includes all macros)

│ ├── 01-registers.nasm # Register definitions (accumulator, base, counter, ...)

│ ├── 04-segments.nasm # Segment definitions

│ ├── 05-data-movement.nasm # move, load, store, etc.

│ ├── 06-arithmetic.nasm # add, subtract, multiply, etc.

│ ├── 07-logic.nasm # logical_and, logical_or, etc.

│ ├── 08-shift-rotate.nasm # shift/rotate instructions

│ ├── 10-jumps.nasm # jump_if_equal, jump_if_greater, etc.

│ ├── 12-procedures.nasm # call_procedure, return_from_procedure

│ ├── 13-stack.nasm # push_onto_stack, pop_from_stack

│ ├── example.asm # Basic usage examples

│ ├── fibonacci.asm # Fibonacci with readable macros

│ ├── fibonacci_raw.asm # Same program, raw NASM (for comparison)

│ ├── structs.asm # C-like structs + nested structs demo

│ ├── sdl_rectangle.asm # SDL2 game demo

│ ├── hello.lisp # rasl demo (every language feature)

│ └── hello.expected # expected output for the test suite

├── compiler/ # rasl: a Lisp that compiles to rasm (Go)

│ ├── codegen.go # symbol table + code emission

items.summary_ko: Readable Assembly는 1000개 이상의 NASM 매크로로 x86-64 명령어 니모닉을 영어 이름으로 바꿔, 문서처럼 읽히는 어셈블리를 작성하게 해주는 프로젝트다. 매크로는 순수 전처리기 방식이라 실행 시 오버헤드가 없다. rasl 컴파일러(Go로 작성)는 리스트, 클로저, GC가 없는 최소 Lisp을 이 매크로 기반의 어셈블리로 바로 컴파일한다.
