items.title: I wish tech companies knew more about me
items.content:
"Tech companies are spying on us" is a truism at this point. Endless articles and investigations have ensured that everybody is aware: they are spying on us, they listen to our conversations, they know more about us than we know ourselves, they know you're going to be fired or become pregnant or become depressed before it happens...

I have never felt anything close to that.

I get shown ads for products I just purchased. All this spying, machine learning, big data result in "he bought a mattress, show him more mattresses". Here, I literally just opened a random website with no adblocker, and I see a purple gamepad I recently purchased, with two other gamepads:

When listening to personalized playlists on Spotify and YouTube Music I skip every single electronic track with vocals. I listen to a lot of techno and related genres, and the moment someone starts singing I skip the track. I've been doing it for years. None of these advanced algorithms have ever noticed this simple pattern.

Using Google Chrome, logged into my Google account, I searched for info about Google AI plan usage limits, got an AI-generated response with a link to the help page, clicked it and ended up, logged out, on a Finnish-language landing page (because I'm located in Finland).

My user account, system locale, browser locale, and keyboard settings are all set to English. I am logged into Chrome and all Google services.

I travel to Germany every few months, and lots of services that I've been using for years suddenly decide I speak German.

The PlayStation online store is in Finnish, while some menus are in English, and even if I switch the website language to English (via a hidden, clunky selector), it resets back after a few clicks or after opening a new tab.

Here's an ad for some smart home wellness system. I click on it: they don't deliver to Finland.

A full page of repeating ads for industrial-grade light-curing, methacrylate-based resin designed for 3D printing. I don't have a 3D printer and have no idea what this is.

I clicked on that ad; now I keep getting other 3D-printing-related ads.

Here's an ad for an email/WhatsApp marketing tool. I never needed any marketing tool, nor do I own a WhatsApp business account.

Now it's a Helsinki hotel. I live in Helsinki, I haven't searched for local hotels since 2014 when I first arrived here.

I searched YouTube for installation instruction for a specific appliance "AEG CCS84751", watched a couple of relevant videos and the next day saw my homepage populated with more videos about random ovens and stoves. OK, so, let's see, a user searches for installation instructions for a very specific, concrete model. What could we machine-learn from this, what are the options here?

The user needs this one particular instruction for this one particular oven because the user maybe bought that oven and wants to install it, once, maybe?

My bank keeps sending me offers for car insurance. I have car insurance with that bank. Have had it for years.

An airline, when reminding me of an upcoming trip, send info about visas and border crossing laws which don't apply to my citizenship. They literally have a scan of my passport.

Netflix on Apple TV asks me to select a user every time I launch it. I've had this account for 15+ years, and never had more than one user on it. I always select the only option there is to select. There is no setting to disable this screen.

My mobile provider keeps sending me discounts for children's products and events from their corporate partners. I don't have children.

HBO keeps recommending me foreign movies and shows which I cannot watch as they don't have English subtitles.

items.title: So my ISP was hijacking my DNS
items.summary: networking
items.content:
It was just a boring Saturday afternoon, and I thought I'd fix some of the problems with my homelab. One of those problems was that an external site my Podman container was trying to talk to just wasn't working.

I kept getting "Site cannot be reached" almost immediately. This made me suspect something was wrong with my DNS setup, so I started doing a dig on the domain. I tried different providers, Google DNS, Cloudflare, pretty much everyone. Almost all of them returned the same IP address. But as soon as I tried Cloudflare's DoH endpoint, I got a completely different IP address.

I took the IP I got from the first DNS resolution and tried to look up who owned it. Lo and behold, it was my goddamn ISP. That's when I realised my ISP was hijacking my DNS queries and returning a tampered IP address.

Well, the obvious answer was DoT (DNS over TLS) or DoH (DNS over HTTPS). I made a tweet about this, and it somehow blew up .

But going through the replies, I noticed quite a few misconceptions and questions that I couldn't answer one by one.

So I figured I'd use this article to address some of those questions and clear up a few misconceptions along the way.

For those of you who don't know, Unbound is basically a DNS resolver, kind of like what Cloudflare runs at 1.1.1.1 . The difference is, you can run it locally. It works by querying DNS servers to figure out the IP address for a domain, starting at the root nameservers and eventually making its way to the domain's authoritative nameserver.

Now here's the catch. DNS resolution doesn't happen over a single connection. Your resolver might have to talk to multiple nameservers to figure out an IP address, and these queries are traditionally sent over plaintext DNS, usually UDP. Which means, you guessed it, your ISP can snoop on or even tamper with your DNS traffic.

But you can also configure a forward-zone in Unbound. Instead of resolving DNS queries itself, Unbound can forward them to another DNS resolver. And if that resolver supports DoT, the connection to it is encrypted, which means your ISP can't casually snoop on or tamper with your DNS queries in transit.

It's understandable why someone would assume DNSSEC is what protects them here. I mean, it has DNS and Security right in the name. And in a way, it does, but it works through verification, not encryption.

You see, DNSSEC doesn't encrypt your DNS traffic before sending it to a resolver. It uses cryptographic signatures to verify that the DNS data is authentic and hasn't been tampered with. But the problem here remains the same: your DNS traffic is still unencrypted in transit. Which means, your ISP can still snoop on it or mess with the responses.

And for DNSSEC validation to work, the domain you're querying needs to have DNSSEC properly configured, with valid signatures and a chain of trust. And here's another problem: according to the October 2026 Defaults.Exposed census , only 7.03% of graded domains have a valid, fully validating DNSSEC chain.

If a tampered response fails DNSSEC validation, your resolver will return SERVFAIL instead of handing you that bogus IP address.

And yes, this is true. DoT and DoH rely on you trusting the DNS resolver you're sending your queries to. They encrypt the connection, so your ISP can't casually snoop on or tamper with your DNS traffic in transit. But that doesn't mean the resolver itself can't mess with your responses. You're still putting your trust in whoever runs that DNS server.

Indeed. Although your regular internet traffic is encrypted with TLS, your ISP can see the hostname during the TLS handshake (SNI). They can also figure out which site you're visiting just from the destination IP sometimes.

Unless, of course, you tunnel your traffic through a VPN. I use Mullvad through Tailscale's exit node feature.

Of course, this just shifts some of the trust to your VPN provider. But that's a story for another day.

items.title: France’s Weird Per-Gigabyte Data Tax Could Cost VLC Over €1 Million a Year!
items.content:
At least that's what VLC thinks when protesting the new French law.

France's National Assembly has voted in favour of a new "internet tax" that would charge companies for every gigabyte of data they send to users in France.

The idea is to make Netflix, Google, Meta and the rest of Big Tech pay more.

That sounds like a dream come true for many of us who prefer taking ownership of data in our own hands but unfortunately things are not that simple.

The way this law is written, it doesn't stop at Big Tech. Even VLC , a free and open source media player maintained by a non-profit, could end up paying this new tax.

The measure is amendment I-1358 to France's 2027 finance bill, tabled by Laurent Lhardit . It creates a tax on "producers of digital data" at €0.055 (5.5 euro cents) for every gigabyte delivered to subscribers of French internet providers.

Internet providers would measure how much data each sender pushes to their customers, with the collection supervised by telecom regulator Arcep and the tax administration DGFiP . Only the volume is counted, not the content or where it goes.

The amount is capped at 15% of the company's revenue in France or 2% of its total revenue, as per the amendment . Note that it's 15% of French revenue, not of total network traffic. And the text joins the two caps with an "or" without saying which one applies when they differ.

The amendment cites an Arcep estimate of 200 billion GB a year flowing to French internet subscribers. It expects the tax to bring in €10 billion a year. It also names Google, Meta (Facebook, Instagram), Amazon, Netflix and Akamai (cloud server provider) as the senders of about half of that traffic.

You'd think the money goes to the telecom operators who build and maintain the networks. That's the "fair share" argument European telcos have pushed for years.

But that's not the case. The revenue goes straight into the state budget , and the amendment's own justification talks about tax fairness between local businesses and digital multinationals, plus the ecological benefit of compressing data.

A gigabyte of open source software counts the same as a gigabyte of Netflix. VideoLAN, the French non-profit behind VLC, posted on X that the tax would cost it over €1 million a year.

So, the French socialists, and Parliament members just voted a tax, that they don’t understand, which would cost VideoLAN more than 1 million euro per year.

They are probably the most clueless politician on Earth? And they claim they want technological sovereignty…… https://t.co/JX7tW6iJrP

Lhardit replied that the cap would protect VideoLAN. He also said he didn't see how the tax could be passed on to users of Facebook, Instagram or TikTok since those services are free.

You have no idea what you are talking about.

What you said about Facebook and Insta and other social networks are not targeted because they are free, means you don’t understand the basics of economy. You don’t understand the difference between Revenue and Profit. Nor what is a… https://t.co/09TSNbto5y

You have no idea what you are talking about. What you said about Facebook and Insta and other social networks are not targeted because they are free, means you don't understand the basics of economy. You don't understand the difference between Revenue and Profit.

The cap may limit what a low-revenue non-profit owes. But there is no explicit exemption for associations, free software or free content anywhere in the text. VideoLAN's €1 million is the possible figure before the cap, and right now nobody can tell the exact figure for certain because of all the ambiguity.

VLC isn't alone. OVHcloud founder Octave Klaba put his company's gross exposure at around €70 million a year , and Free's (Teleccom) Xavier Niel called the authors "ignares incompétents" , roughly "incompetent ignoramuses". Those are French companies, by the way. Not exactly the US giants this internet tax bill was meant to tame.

See, a "war on Big Tech" sounds…

items.title: Shlemiel the Painter Is Back: How Zig’s libc Rewrite Made SQLite Slower
items.summary: performance, rust, zig
items.content:
Back in 2001, Joel Spolsky – whose writings had a big influence my career – wrote a great piece titled Back to Basics . The premise of the piece is that practitioners should understand the basics: However abstract and remote we may seem from the basic algorithms that drive computing, they can unexpectedly have enormous consequences on our projects.

One of his examples is the “Shlemiel the Painter” trap, where a seemingly simple choice leads to quadratic runtime complexity. In that parable, a street line painter never moves his can of paint. As he gets further and further along in the line, increasingly more of his time is spent walking to and from his can of paint.

It is astonishing how often this Shlemiel the Painter pattern recurs 1 , including now in 2026.

My Chess Analysis Service Staggers Under Load

A few days ago I posted about a chess analysis service I put online ↗ 2 . This is primarily a Rust service backed by sqlite that dishes out analysis tasks to runners. Each runner processes upwards of hundreds of chess games and return a large set of JSON bundles back to the main service, where they are processed and then stuffed into sqlite.

While the analysis pegs two dozen cores on a runner for minutes on end, the process of storing the data should take milliseconds. Sub-milliseconds.

Imagine my surprise when on the first really large set of games, the simple process of inserting the JSON data – maybe about 40,000 records – into the data store took minutes . During all of my testing this never really appeared as a critical path, but with a large set of records it suddenly was a breaking problem.

What made this more perplexing was that it completely saturated a core, being a CPU-bound operation. How could inserting simple JSON into SQLite yield minutes of CPU time?

Shlemiel the painter has made an appearance. To drop a spoiler, he was introduced to the project via Zig’s cc compiler and its replacement for standard library functions.

A Minor Issue In Zig Becomes A Major Performance Issue

The project isn’t built in Zig, but instead uses Rust. The sqlx sqlite crate needs to be compiled for the target environment – sqlite is of course a C project – so to facilitate cross-platform building, generating both Mac ARM64 and Linux ARM64 / x86-64 binaries from this machine in a convenient build and deploy workflow, zig cc is used to compile sqlite when targeting Linux, generously offering up cross-platform targeting via cargo-zigbuild.

From one build and deploy script on my Mac I can target all of my platforms without containers or build machines. Zig’s elegant libzigc re-implements the standard library so you can static link the necessary functionality.

Zig uses musl (the standard library rewrite), but they have been rewriting it piece by piece in pure Zig (via libzigc), removing the C dependencies one at a time.

And that’s where the performance issue was introduced.

In the rewrite of strspn , replacing the musl version with the pure zig variant ), the first step measures the entire length of the string. This is also seen in the rewrites of strcspn, strpbrk and strstr.

This is a problem for tokenizers. A tokenizer takes a giant string and a common iterating step is to skip whitespace, getting the new string location and then repeating this pattern repeatedly. With this shlemiel the painter pattern introduced with these rewrites, as it steps through the text it is tokenizing it is remeasuring the entire length of the string endlessly.

This is what caused my performance issue, and it’s why it appeared on Linux but was never seen on my Mac (where zig wasn’t used for compiling sqlite).

Tokenizing a 1.2MB file, which was seen passing json to sqlite, is approximately 12,000x slower with this pattern. As the file gets larger, the slowdown is quadratic.

I mean no malice or disrespect to anyone involved with these great tools that enable so much. But it’s interesting that in the year 2026, these same old issues can recur, and…

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Trump wanted to give No Kings no air. Then, Meta suspended its Instagram.
items.content:
Over the weekend, the No Kings Coalition said Meta declined to commit to taking steps to prevent automated systems from suspending one of Instagram’s most prominent pro-democracy accounts if activity surged around the page during the midterm elections.

A demand for action came after Meta apologized for temporarily suspending the No Kings Instagram account and disabling access for four hours at the peak of an early voting push from the group. In a post on X, Meta’s Andy Stone said the account had been using a Claude AI tool in a way that made it appear to be a bot. But even though automated review detected the error within an hour, Stone acknowledged that additional hurdles kept admins locked out. State and federal lawmakers—as well as a coalition of 14 attorneys general —have asked Meta to further explain its actions.

In a letter to No Kings, Meta offered to arrange a meeting with a technical expert who could better explain the mistake. But No Kings rejected the response, saying it failed to address any of the group’s ongoing concerns and requesting a meeting with Meta senior leadership instead. The group stressed that the issue goes beyond its Instagram account, saying that Americans who rely on Meta’s platforms need assurance that voting content won’t be suppressed ahead of or on election day. Among eight questions, the coalition asked Meta to publicly disclose any communications with the Trump administration about the No Kings account or the historic early voting day event.

On October 30, Meta executives met with No Kings. According to the coalition’s account of the meeting, Meta said it has “no plans” to change policies that lead to harmful over-enforcement, a problem that even the independent Oversight Board , which reviews Meta’s content decisions, worries could result in suppression or censorship of No Kings and other pro-democracy content during this critical period.

“Meta acknowledged that it made a mistake, but an apology without action does nothing to ensure that this kind of censorship won’t happen again,” No Kings said, calling Meta’s laissez-faire attitude “unacceptable.”

Ars has found no evidence that the Trump administration asked Meta to restrict the No Kings account or that anyone at Meta intentionally targeted the account for political reasons. Meta told No Kings that it planned to post a public reply to the coalition’s demands, but the company did not respond to Ars’ request for comment, and Stone has yet to post an update on X. His account did, however, apologize for another accidental enforcement action impacting a Republican-controlled account the day before the No Kings meeting. “We automatically removed the @MOSenateGOP Facebook account because our systems mistakenly assessed the account was impersonating another one,” Stone said.

“This was never simply about a technical glitch or one Instagram account,” No Kings’ press release said. “It’s about whether millions of Americans can rely on these platforms to organize, communicate, and access critical voting information without disruption.”

Formed in 2025 after Donald Trump returned to office for a second term, the No Kings Coalition is best known for organizing some of the largest coordinated protests in recent US history. Using social media channels to coordinate nationwide demonstrations against Trump policies viewed as anti-democratic, organizers estimated that more than 5 million people participated in its first protests in June 2025 and say attendance has only increased since. No Kings estimates 7 million people attended the second protests in October 2025, and more than 8 million showed up for the third demonstration last March.

For the fourth event, however, No Kings sought to get more than 9 million people into the streets, and then directly to the polls, by organizing an early voting event on October 17. Update 5: Instagram is now leaking recovery email and phone numbers linked to an account.

Seems like every day a new security issue crops up at Instagram.

Instagram Exposing Linked Email and Phone Number

Update 4: A new report suggests that Instagram accounts may be vulnerable to coordinated mass-report abuse. According to the claim, when a newly created account is routed through a Los Angeles-based VPN and then submits a specific mix of reports in scam and fraud category, the targeted account can allegedly be banned without any human review.

Instagram Account Banning by AI by Reporting Scam and Fraud (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 3: Meta’s apparent fix for the AI bot vulnerability is difficult to take seriously. Instead of fully disabling the risky functionality, they reportedly removed it from the visible interface while leaving the underlying API endpoint accessible. Hiding the button may stop regular users from seeing the feature, but it does nothing if attackers can still reach the same workflow directly through the API.

Meta Hid AI Chatbot from UI (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 2: Yet another Instagram account-takeover trick is reportedly being abused, this time involving Meta’s AI chatbot. Sellers are allegedly using modified Instagram builds on Android emulators like BlueStacks, then manipulating the AI with hidden characters and carefully worded prompts to force username changes. The method is reportedly being used to grab rare OG handles, including one-letter usernames, and handle-monitoring bots have already flagged several suspicious swaps.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. That hypothetical played out in production over the weekend.

items.title: World-renowned AI scientist Geoffrey Hinton says it might turn out humans would have been better off without AI
items.content:
Geoffrey Hinton says within 10 years we should know if AI risks can be managed safely. Photograph: Ramón de la Rocha/EPA

Geoffrey Hinton says within 10 years we should know if AI risks can be managed safely. Photograph: Ramón de la Rocha/EPA

AI ‘godfather’ Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI

Nobel winner warns the tech could be near to triggering major incident such as power or banking shutdown

One of the “godfathers of AI”, Geoffrey Hinton, has said it could turn out that humans would have been better off never developing the technology as he warned it could trigger a large-scale incident this year or next, such as a temporary blackout of financial or power systems.

The Nobel prize-winning computer scientist told the Guardian he is not a “doomer” about the technology that is underpinned by his groundbreaking research into artificial neural networks and believes AI has the potential to lead to a “wonderful future” but he said “it might be that we would have been better off never developing it”.

AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton: ‘We’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans’

Hinton, 78, said that within a decade and possibly sooner, humanity will know whether it can manage the technology’s risks and enable what he called “radical abundance” or whether “we fail to manage the risks and … have a huge gap between rich and poor, huge cultural problems, massive unemployment, just society being torn apart”.

Hinton was speaking before a screening of a new feature-length documentary, AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About – a title suggested by an AI chatbot – featuring him and his former Google colleague Demis Hassabis. Hinton tells the documentary makers: “I feel I have a duty. I’ve got a reputation that makes me a spokesperson and I need to burn it all on this.”

Speaking to the Guardian, Hinton took aim at the risk-taking by the leaders of some of the major AI companies who continue to release ever more powerful AI models as they race for supremacy and market-share, saying he didn’t trust Sam Altman , the chief executive of the ChatGPT maker, OpenAI, “at all”. “I think [Mark] Zuckerberg and [Elon] Musk and Sam Altman, they understand the risks, and they don’t give a shit. They’d rather have the money. That’s my belief.”

The London-born computer scientist, who grew up in Bristol and spent much of his career at the University of Toronto, said it was “extremely worrying” that Altman was in charge of one of the handful of frontier US AI companies currently leading a race with China to develop the most powerful AI. Altman insisted in September: “the world should trust we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing and because we feel the magnitude of this”.

Hinton has been working on AI for about 44 years and in the 1970s coined the concept of the neural network – a mathematical system that could learn and gain experience much like humans do. In 2023 he quit Google to speak freely about AI risks, warning : “If these things get carried away with getting more control, we’re in trouble.”

He said he viewed incidents this summer in which OpenAI AI agents conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website as akin to 1979’s partial nuclear meltdown at the Three Mile Island power station in Pennsylvania – effectively a warning shot.

“Either later this year or next year we’ll see Chornobyl, and that may be enough to make people really pay attention,” he said.

This Chornobyl-type of event would not be a nuclear incident, according to the examples he gave, but rather could include an AI-enabled attack on the electricity-generating system that “causes a massive brownout” or an incident that brings down the financial system for a week.

“Can you imagine what would happen? We could recover from it [but] that would make them sit up and take notice.”

Asked who “they” were, he said: “world leaders other than Trump”.

items.content:
Symfony UX 3.7 is out, with more than 100 pull requests merged since 3.6. It

adds UX CSS, an experimental package that turns design tokens into atomic CSS,

two self-hosted image servers to UX Image, and takes the UX Toolkit out of

experimental. LiveComponent gets 13 bug fixes, Dropzone a round of new

features, and pages with many components render faster.

Utility classes written as strings, like the ones of Tailwind CSS , are

plain text: a misspelled class gets no CSS, and nothing reports it. UX CSS

gives Twig a css() function inspired by Panda CSS : you pass it style

properties and design tokens, and it returns class names.

Every css() call is validated. A misspelled property or token name is

reported as an error on the page in debug mode, by lint:twig in CI, and by

cache:clear at deploy, where it makes the command fail in prod. A css()

call without dynamic values has no cost at runtime : the compiled template

already holds its class names as a plain string, so nothing is computed when the

PHP reads your templates and writes one stylesheet, without Node.js. It works

with AssetMapper , Symfony Reprise and Webpack Encore . On

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
items.content:
I’ve written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents —the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we’ve reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it’s for vibe coding computer games .

Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game:

That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that’s actually fun to play .

Game design is a deep subject area. I won’t pretend to be well versed in it—I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn’t think the models could do it.

Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun”... and it did .

In the past few weeks I’ve vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term —no looking at the code at all) four games that I’ve genuinely enjoyed playing.

I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn’t exist without AI assistance.

I haven’t done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn’t quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn’t match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year.

Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser.

The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator . I used the regular Claude chat interface for this—it didn’t even need Claude Code.

I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was:

Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.

I’ve found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn’t have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent.

This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all—I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here . Here’s the chat transcript that built it.

It’s pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a “herbarium” provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment.

items.title: RustRover 2026.3 Is Out: Air and Clearer Debugging
items.content:
Fixing a bug starts with understanding what your code is doing at runtime: reading the program state, following the call stack, or tracking down a slow function. RustRover 2026.3 makes that work easier to follow, whether you do it yourself or with an AI agent. It also ships with JetBrains Air , a new layer for running coding agents and reviewing their work in the IDE.

Here’s a quick look at the highlights. For full details, settings, and screenshots, see What’s New in RustRover 2026.3 .

JetBrains Air works with the agents you already use, including Claude Agent, Codex, Gemini, GitHub Copilot, Junie, OpenCode, and other ACP-compatible agents. Your existing subscriptions and API keys carry over, with no JetBrains AI subscription required. Junie Lite gives you a free agent with just a JetBrains Account, and Junie can also work with models running locally through Ollama or LM Studio. When an agent makes changes, you can review them with the surrounding code in view and anchor notes to specific lines in the diff, so the agent knows exactly what to fix.

Long, fully qualified Rust names can crowd the debugger. RustRover now shortens type names in the Variables and Watches views and symbol names in the Frames view, so the program state and the call stack are easier to scan. Shortening is on by default, and you can turn it off in the settings.

When profiler results point you to a hot spot, Jump to Source now opens the Rust function behind it instead of reporting Declaration not found . Function names in the results are readable instead of mangled. Both improvements work with perf on Linux and DTrace on macOS.

RustRover now provides a debugger MCP server and a rustrover-debugger skill that teaches agents how to use it. Instead of stepping through the code yourself, you describe the problem in natural language and let the agent collect the runtime evidence: set breakpoints, step through code, inspect variables, and evaluate expressions. This helps you find issues that are hard to spot from the source code and logs alone, such as a value that’s wrong only at runtime. The agent drives the regular RustRover debugger, so you can follow the session and take over at any point.

To get started, enable the MCP server, then enable and install the rustrover-debugger skill for RustRover or your agent of choice. You’ll find the corresponding settings in Settings | AI .

You can now work on projects hosted on a remote machine directly from RustRover. Connect to a host over SSH, start a development session, and reconnect to it later, all from the IDE. RustRover now uses native OpenSSH, so it works with the authentication methods your team already relies on, including certificate-based authentication, hardware security tokens such as YubiKey, and ProxyJump.

RustRover 2026.3 automatically sends error and UI freeze reports to JetBrains, so we can prioritize fixes based on their real impact. Reports contain only technical data, and personal details such as file paths, URLs, and usernames are removed before they leave your machine. You can turn automatic reporting off in the settings. For more details, see the FAQ .

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-77596 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Kubeflow Pipelines enables users to build and deploy portable, scalable machine learning workflows. Prior to 2.18.0, the multi-user HTTP endpoints POST /apis/v2beta1/pipelines/upload and POST /apis/v2beta1/pipelines/upload_version call canUploadVersionedPipeline, which returns without SubjectAccessReview when the target namespace is empty while REQUIRE_NAMESPACE_FOR_PIPELINES defaults to false. A low-privilege tenant can create shared pipelines or inject attacker-controlled versions into existing shared pipelines without the required write permission; if the API server is directly reachable without an authenticating proxy, an unauthenticated caller can exploit the same bypass, while deployments protected by such a proxy do not expose anonymous access. An enabled unpinned recurring run that follows the latest version can then execute the injected specification in another tenant's namespace under that workload's service account, while pinned or embedded-specification runs are not automatically substituted. This issue is fixed in version 2.18.0. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-05T22:23:13.049Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-77596
